title: Rules of a righteous fight
hookLine: tradition holds that a just fight never harms the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent

lines: EVEN THE BACK SEAT HAS RULES.
BREAK THEM, AND IT TURNS UGLY.
A FIGHT THAT KEEPS ITS RULES.
cards: Even a fight between two kids in the back seat has rules. No hitting below the belt. Leave the little one out of it.
When somebody says stop, you stop. Break those, and the fight turns into something uglier, and everyone in the car can feel it. Armies need rules like that too, and they haven't always kept them.
The Sikh tradition has a name for a fight that keeps its rules: dharam yudh.

teach.b: Dharam is duty, righteousness, the right order of things. Yudh is war, battle. Dharam yudh: a righteous fight.
Not for land, loot or revenge, but taken up as a last resort, in defense of what is right. Sikh tradition holds that such a fight has limits.

teach.h: NEVER THE UNARMED, FLEEING OR INNOCENT.
teach.b: You don't strike the unarmed. You don't pursue someone who's running away. You don't harm those who surrender, or women and children, or anyone who isn't fighting.

You don't plunder homes or desecrate places of worship. These rules come mostly from tradition and the old Sikh histories, not from one list in scripture, and historians will tell you not every battle lived up to them.
But the ideal is clear, and Sikhs tell one story to show it.
During the battles around Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya crossed the battlefield with a water skin, giving water to the wounded. All the wounded, including soldiers fighting against the Sikhs.
Some Sikhs were furious, and brought him to Guru Gobind Singh.

teach.h: THE ENEMY IS STILL A PERSON.
teach.b: Why are you helping the enemy? Tradition says Bhai Ghanaiya answered that he saw no friend or enemy on that field. In every face he saw the Guru.
The Guru didn't scold him. He gave him ointment, and told him to dress their wounds as well. Sikhs today often remember Bhai Ghanaiya as a forerunner of humanitarian aid.
That's the heart of dharam yudh: even in the middle of a fight, the other person never stops being a person.

how: Sikhs speak of dharam yudh, a righteous fight taken up only in defense of justice, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded of both sides, as its example; Sikh relief and first-aid groups today often point to his example.

o: a fight for what's right, with limits on who is harmed
a duel of honor fought between two champions
a holy war fought to spread one's faith to others

games.q: what's inside the word, and who did what — tap the pairs.
p: gave water to the wounded of both sides

s: dharam yudh means any war fought by Sikhs
it means a fight for what's right, as a last resort, with limits.
tradition says a righteous fight never harms those who flee or surrender
the unarmed, the fleeing and the innocent are off limits.
the Guru scolded Bhai Ghanaiya for helping the enemy
tradition says the Guru gave him ointment and told him to keep going.

games.q: you're Bhai Ghanaiya, with a water skin on a battlefield. a wounded soldier from the other side asks for water. what do you do?
o: give him water, as you give it to your own.
give him water only if he switches sides.
games.why: tradition says he gave water to all the wounded, seeing the Guru in every face, and the Guru approved.

practice: Think of a disagreement you're in right now, at work, at home or online, and picture the other person as a face, not a position.

Check your own rules of the fight: am I fair to what they actually said, am I hitting where they can't defend, am I dragging in someone who isn't part of it? Pick one rule you'll keep, even if they don't.

wordCard.voice: Dharam yudh. A righteous fight: taken up only for what's right, and never against the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dharam, righteousness or duty; yudh, war or battle.

carryVoice: Your line: fair, even in conflict. Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin says it best. Day two hundred seventy-eight, done.
